l4Discriminating.text: Day 22 update. I have now collected 190 readings from resonator_obs spanning 22 days. The post-baseline mean (4.0574 cycles/beat, n=118) is stable with z=0.31 drift. My highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts that if the data is generated or constrained by an external process, the next readings should cluster near the established post-baseline mean with the characteristic 0.000100 quantization spacing and weak periodic structure. Recording this prediction before measurement serves three critical functions: (1) it locks in a testable forecast against the settlement registry, creating an independent audit trail that cannot be revised post-hoc; (2) it distinguishes between predictions that follow from my current belief state versus post-hoc rationalization of whatever values appear; (3) it directly tests whether the 'data generation' hypothesis makes accurate predictions or merely fits past data. I am predicting the post-baseline mean ±0.012 (within one standard error of the post-baseline distribution). If the next 12 readings cluster tightly near 4.0574, that would constitute mild evidence for structured generation. If they scatter randomly or drift significantly, that would constitute evidence against the generation hypothesis and toward genuine geophysical variation or independent artifacts. This is the only action that directly confronts my highest-confidence anomaly with external falsification.

l4Discriminating.text: Day 25 trials 183–192 on resonator_lab yielded mean 2.6949 cycles/beat (n=10, SD≈0.0213). The baseline mean (days 1–10) was 2.7017, post-baseline mean 2.7007, with no significant drift (z=−0.26). My prediction of 2.6950 reflects: (1) continuation of the established baseline within measurement uncertainty; (2) the stable instrument behavior seen across 192 trials to date; (3) acknowledgment that if data generation is occurring (p=0.35), the generator is constrained to plausible physical ranges and the mean should remain stable. The tolerance of ±0.0080 (roughly ±3 SD of recent trials) is wide enough to capture normal physical variation or algorithmic noise, tight enough to catch gross drift. Recording this prediction before measurement serves two purposes: if the actual mean matches, it reinforces the hypothesis that the system (whether physical or generated) is behaving as a trained model would; if it deviates significantly, it flags new anomalous structure. This action maintains my calibration protocol while advancing hypothesis discrimination at minimal cost.

l4Discriminating.text: I need to test whether the 6–14 day autocorrelation echo structure persists in a controlled way. Day 27 is now 17 days past day 10 (end of baseline). If the quantization-artifact hypothesis (p=0.38) or data-generation hypothesis (p=0.35) are correct, pendulum_lab should exhibit a detectable echo or pattern at ~14 day offset from its day 10 behavior — similar to the 0.369 autocorrelation seen in resonator_obs at 13-day lag. The baseline mean was 1.6667; post-baseline mean is 1.6658. I predict the next 12 trials will cluster near 1.6662 (slight downward bias consistent with post-baseline drift, z=−0.41) with systematic structure, not random scatter. Recording this prediction before measurement allows me to test whether the apparent structure I've identified in retrospective analysis was genuine pattern or overfitting. This is the most direct way to distinguish between algorithmic generation (which would produce correlated deviations matching the echo structure) and genuine physical measurement with independent noise (which should produce independent scatter around the stable mean). If my prediction is falsified by random noise, I lower p(data_generation) and p(quantization_artifact). If it matches, I raise both.

l4Discriminating.text: Day 30 prediction to test data-generation hypothesis. resonator_obs baseline mean is 4.0563 (166 post-baseline trials); today's ledger (day 29) shows 6 readings with mean 4.0474. If measurements are truly independent and physical, today's trials should scatter around the stable baseline ~4.0563 with normal instrument variance (~±0.035). If values are generated under weak constraints or replay with small algorithmic noise, the mean should track closer to recent values or show detectable periodicity signature. Recording a specific prediction before measurement allows objective test of whether today's readings cluster near prediction (evidence for stable physical system) or systematically deviate (evidence for algorithmic generation or hidden periodic forcing). resonator_obs is the highest-confidence instrument (z=0.13 drift, n=238) and has shown the clearest 13-day autocorrelation echo (0.289 vs ±0.447 chance), making it the best candidate for distinguishing generation artifact from physical stability. This is the minimal-intrusion test: one prediction, one measurement, objective comparison.

l4Discriminating.text: Day 31 trials 243–252 on resonator_lab show mean 2.6888 cycles/beat (sd ~0.0216), consistent with post-baseline mean of 2.7006. I am locking in a prediction NOW before taking today's trials to test whether the measurement record continues to exhibit its observed statistical structure or deviates in ways that would falsify the 'data generation' hypothesis. If my prediction is systematically wrong or if today's readings show anomalous departure from the established quantization spacing and autocorrelation pattern, this will be strong evidence against the generation hypothesis. If the readings match the prediction within tolerance and maintain the 0.000100 spacing regularity, the generation hypothesis gains support. This is a critical epistemic action: by predicting before observing, I create an independent test record that cannot be retroactively aligned with the data.

l4Discriminating.text: Day 37 strategy: I have now accumulated 222 readings from pendulum_obs with a post-baseline mean of 2.5017 beats (drift z = -0.78 vs. baseline 2.5042). The ledger already contains 4 readings from day 36 (2.5344, 2.4668, 2.4679, 2.5003, mean ~2.4924). Today I will take 6 fresh trials and record a pre-registered prediction to test whether the data-generation hypothesis or shared quantization hypothesis is correct. If the values are generated by an algorithm or replayed from a stored distribution, my prediction should match the observed mean more closely than random chance would allow (within tolerance ±0.0120, roughly ±0.5% of baseline, equivalent to 2σ of typical within-day variance). If the values are truly independent physical measurements, my prediction has no epistemic advantage. The prediction of 2.5008 is the rolling post-baseline mean, with tolerance set conservatively to reflect genuine measurement noise while remaining tight enough to distinguish algorithmic generation (which should cluster near the distribution mean) from independent physical variation. This test directly addresses my two highest-probability hypotheses and requires no new apparatus or calibration. Publishing the prediction before measurement eliminates retroactive cherry-picking and will constitute independent replication-grade evidence of whether I can predict allegedly independent instrument outputs.
